task_title: Timed Turns to Magnetic Compass Headings
area: Area VI. Flight by Reference to Instruments
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how the magnetic compass works and every error it has, calibrate the turn coordinator (or turn needle) left and right with the full panel and the clock, work out and fly timed turns at standard and half standard rate, fly compass turns to a heading full panel and partial panel with either IFH roll-out rule, demonstrate it while explaining, and analyze and correct the calibration, timing, coordination and trim errors an examiner simulates.
why: In most small airplanes the magnetic compass is the only direction instrument that does not depend on other instruments or a power source, and many pilots use it only to set the heading indicator, though knowing its errors lets a pilot turn to and hold headings with it [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. When the heading indicator or the AHRS fails, the clock, the turn instrument and the compass are what is left for turning to a heading [[23:214|IFH 7-53]]. The CFII PTS wants this taught full panel and partial panel because instrument-rated pilots have died maneuvering in cloud with failed gyros or a lost electronic display (CFII PTS, Emphasis on Attitude Instrument Flying and Partial Panel Skills).

warmup: Think first: your instrument student, partial panel near 41° north, is told to turn left from east to north on the magnetic compass. She rolls into 30° of bank to get it over with and rolls out the moment the card shows N. What will the card do during that turn, where will she end up, and which two things would you teach before she tries again?

key_terms.def: Two small magnets on a float in compass fluid; the card is read against the lubber line, seen from behind [[23:106|IFH 5-11]]. In most small airplanes it is the only direction instrument independent of other instruments and power sources [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].
The reference line across the compass window that the heading is read against [[23:106|IFH 5-11]].
The angle between true and magnetic north; it does not change with the airplane's heading [[23:107|IFH 5-12]].
Compass error caused by magnetic fields in the airplane; it changes with heading, not with location, and what cannot be removed goes on the correction card [[23:107|IFH 5-12]] [[23:108|IFH 5-13]].

The angle of Earth's magnetic field to the surface, which grows toward the magnetic poles. The compass reads correctly only with the card horizontal; tilted, it feels the vertical pull of the field, which leads to the turning errors [[1:227|PHAK 8-25]] [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]].
Starting a turn from north, the compass lags or shows a turn the other way; starting from south, it shows more turn than is happening [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].
On east or west headings, accelerating shows a turn toward north and decelerating a turn toward south [[23:109|IFH 5-14]].
A mix of the other errors that swings the card back and forth around the heading; use the average of the swings [[23:109|IFH 5-14]].
A heading change of a set number of degrees using the clock and the turn coordinator: 45° in 15 seconds at standard rate, 45° in 30 seconds at half standard rate [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].
Holding the indicated standard rate and checking the heading every 10 seconds by the clock; standard rate is 30° per 10 seconds, and each direction is checked [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].
The turn-and-slip indicator's rate gyro senses rotation about the vertical axis only. On a 2 MIN dial one needle width is standard rate; on a 4 MIN dial, two widths [[23:116|IFH 5-21]].
A turn to a heading on the magnetic compass, rolling out early or late to allow for its turning error [[23:182|IFH 7-21]] [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

chunks.title: What the examiner looks for in Task F

body.p: **Teaching timed turns to magnetic compass headings** is Task F of Area VI. You describe the compass's operating characteristics and errors, the calibration of the turn coordinator's miniature aircraft right and left with full panel and the clock, and full panel and partial panel compass turns to a heading; then the common errors (incorrect calibration, improper timing, uncoordinated controls, improper trim); then you demonstrate while explaining, and analyze and correct simulated errors (CFII PTS, Area VI, Task F). A PTS footnote says that if the test airplane has a turn needle, the turn needle replaces the miniature aircraft of the turn coordinator (CFII PTS, Task F, footnote 1).

The Area NOTE has the evaluator select Task H and at least one other Task, and you teach with the method you chose, primary and supporting or control and performance (CFII PTS, Area VI NOTE). The general Area VI material is in FII.VI.A: the two methods, the grading words, the exchange of controls and simulating failures safely. Turns themselves are in the sibling lesson FII.VI.B, which uses timed turns only as a partial panel tool. FII.II.A covers the compass as an instrument, the Instrument lesson IR.IV.A covers the pilot's side, and the CFI lesson AI.XI.D teaches compass and timed turns to VFR learners.

callout.text: The rule: for IFR flight the airplane needs the day VFR instruments [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(1)]], which include a magnetic direction indicator [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)(3)]], plus a gyroscopic rate-of-turn indicator (not required in an airplane with a third attitude instrument system usable through 360 degrees of pitch and roll) [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(3)]], a slip-skid indicator [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(4)]], and a clock showing hours, minutes and seconds with a sweep-second pointer or digital presentation [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(6)]]. In a typical trainer, every tool in this Task is required IFR equipment.

Application: open the ground lesson with the reason, not the errors. "The day your heading indicator quits in a cloud, these three things still work: the clock, the turn coordinator and the compass. Today you learn to turn with them."

check.q: The examiner says the test airplane has a turn-and-slip indicator, not a turn coordinator. What changes in Task F?
check.a: Only the instrument: the PTS footnote puts the turn needle in place of the turn coordinator's miniature aircraft (CFII PTS, Task F, footnote 1), so you calibrate and time turns on the needle. It senses rotation about the vertical axis only, so it shows no roll [[23:116|IFH 5-21]].

body.p: **Operating characteristics of the magnetic compass.** Two small magnets are attached to a metal float sealed in a bowl of fluid similar to kerosene. The card wrapped around the float is read through a window against the lubber line. It has letters for the cardinal points and a number every 30° with the last zero left off (3 = 30°, 33 = 330°); long marks are 10°, short marks 5° [[23:106|IFH 5-11]].

bullets: Mounting: the float rides on a pivot in a jewel cup and can rotate and tilt up to about 18° of bank. At steeper banks the readings are erratic and unpredictable [[23:106|IFH 5-11]].

Read from behind: the pilot sees the back of the card, so on north the 33 sits to the right of N even though east is to the right. The card stays still while the housing and pilot turn around it [[23:106|IFH 5-11]]. That is why it is easy to start a turn the wrong way [[23:110|IFH 5-15]].

Built for level flight: the center of gravity is below the pivot so the card turns only in the horizontal plane. It reads correctly only while the card is horizontal; tilted, it is affected by the vertical part of Earth's field. Near the magnetic poles it is unusable [[1:227|PHAK 8-25]] [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]].
Fluid: the housing is completely full, a diaphragm or bellows takes up expansion, and the fluid damps the float's oscillation [[23:106|IFH 5-11]].

Vertical card compass: a gear-driven dial with a symbolic airplane as the lubber line and eddy-current damping; it removes some of the errors and the confusion of the backward card [[23:110|IFH 5-15]].

body.p: Preflight items for this lesson: the compass is full of fluid and the correction card is in place and current, and the clock is set and running [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. Before taxi, the card moves freely and agrees with a known heading such as the runway; set the heading indicator to it [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. On glass panels pilots tend to leave the standby instruments and the compass out of the scan, partly because of where the standbys sit [[23:161|IFH 6-28]].

callout.text: Application: hold a hand-held compass, or a picture of one, in front of the learner and turn it. Watching the card stand still while the case turns explains the backward numbers faster than words.

check.q: Your student says the compass is useless in her 30° bank partial panel turns. What do you answer?
check.a: The float tilts only to about 18° of bank; steeper, the readings are erratic and unpredictable [[23:106|IFH 5-11]]. Keep compass turns shallow and read the compass once straight, level and unaccelerated [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

chunks.title: Errors of the compass: variation, deviation and oscillation

body.p: **Errors of the magnetic compass**, part one: the errors that are there even in straight, steady flight.

head: Error
Cause
What to teach
rows: Variation
The magnetic north pole is some 1,300 miles from the geographic pole; the angle between true and magnetic directions is variation [[23:107|IFH 5-12]]
The same on every heading along an isogonic line. Near Washington, D.C., with 10° west variation, true 180 is magnetic 190 [[23:107|IFH 5-12]]
Deviation
Magnetic fields from current in the structure, nearby wiring or magnetized parts [[23:107|IFH 5-12]]
Different on each heading, not affected by location. Swinging the compass minimizes it; what is left goes on the correction card [[23:107|IFH 5-12]] [[23:108|IFH 5-13]]
Equipment effects

Radios, deicing, pitot heat, radar or magnetic cargo [[1:227|PHAK 8-25]]; an electrically heated windshield can cause up to 40° [[1:201|PHAK 7-41]]; precipitation static can cause erroneous readings [[23:246|IFH 9-3]]
Use the card row for the configuration you fly; Figure 5-19 has rows for radios on and off [[23:108|IFH 5-13]]
Oscillation
A combination of the other errors that swings the card back and forth around the heading [[23:109|IFH 5-14]]
Set the heading indicator to the average of the swings [[23:109|IFH 5-14]]

body.p: The order of corrections: true course ± variation = magnetic course, then magnetic course ± deviation = compass course. In the IFH example, true 180 plus 10° variation is magnetic 190, and deviation of -2° gives a compass course of 188 [[23:108|IFH 5-13]]. On the card in Figure 5-19, magnetic 120 with the radios on is flown as 123 on the compass [[23:108|IFH 5-13]].

Why it matters in this Task: when a timed turn is flown without the heading indicator, the compass checks it afterward, taking deviation into account [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. On the Figure 5-19 card, magnetic 090 with the radios on is steered as 095 [[23:108|IFH 5-13]], so a learner who rolls out on 090 by the compass is about 5° off.

callout.text: True ± variation = magnetic. Magnetic ± deviation = compass. Reverse the steps to go back [[23:108|IFH 5-13]].

check.q: Radios on, your learner checks a timed turn to 270 on the compass and reads 271. Using Figure 5-19, did the turn work?
check.a: Yes. The card says steer 271 for magnetic 270 with the radios on [[23:108|IFH 5-13]], so 271 on the compass is magnetic 270. Checking a timed turn on the compass means allowing for deviation [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

chunks.title: Errors of the compass in flight: acceleration and turning

body.p: **Errors of the magnetic compass**, part two: the ones that show up as you maneuver, which is why a compass turn needs a plan. Magnetic dip and inertia acting on the low-slung float cause them, and the turning errors grow near either pole [[23:108|IFH 5-13]] [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]].

body.p: Why acceleration error happens: the float is pendulous, so its aft end tilts up when accelerating and down when decelerating, and dip and inertia then swing the card [[23:108|IFH 5-13]] [[23:109|IFH 5-14]]. Why turning error happens: as the airplane turns, the force from magnetic dip swings the float and gives a false turn indication [[23:108|IFH 5-13]] [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]].

callout.text: Application: demonstrate ANDS in VMC on a west heading. Add power and hold altitude while the learner watches the card swing toward north, then reduce power and watch it swing south. Repeat on north, where the IFH says no error results [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

check.q: Partial panel on 090, your student levels off and lets the speed build. The compass swings. Is the airplane turning?
check.a: Not necessarily. On an east or west heading, acceleration gives a north turn indication [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. Check the turn coordinator and ball, and read the compass again when straight, level and unaccelerated [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

chunks.title: The IFH errata and the two IFH roll-out rules

body.p: **The IFH errata first.** FAA's errata to the Instrument Flying Handbook (dated July 2, 2014) removes the references to Figures 5-20A and 5-20B from the northerly and southerly turning error text on IFH 5-13, and says to disregard Figure 5-20 on IFH 5-14 because its graphics are inaccurate [[23:108|IFH 5-13]] [[23:109|IFH 5-14]]. Do not teach from that figure. The PHAK prints the same drawing as its Figure 8-36 [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]]. The errata covers only the IFH, but Application: since the drawing is the same, leave the PHAK one out too.

IFH 5-13 also has a typo the errata does not list: its southerly example reads "15° + 15° + 30°" [[23:108|IFH 5-13]]. The PHAK prints the same example correctly: near 30° latitude, stop the turn 15 + 15 = 30 degrees after passing the desired heading [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]].
The IFH then gives two different rules for where to stop a compass turn. They agree on the direction, stop early turning to north and go past turning to south, but not on the amount:

head: Rule A: IFH 5-13 (same in PHAK 8-26)
Rule B: IFH 7-22
rows: Turning to north
Stop the turn 15° plus half the latitude before the heading [[23:108|IFH 5-13]]
Start the roll-out early by the latitude plus the normal roll-out lead (half the bank) [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]
Turning to south
Let the card pass the heading by 15° plus half the latitude [[23:108|IFH 5-13]] [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]]
Keep turning until the compass passes south by the latitude minus the normal roll-out lead [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]
Bank assumed
None stated
Turning to east or west
Not covered
From a northerly heading start the roll-out 10° to 12° early, from a southerly heading about 5° early; interpolate other headings [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]
Example to north
At 30°, 15° bank: from east start at 037, from west at 323 [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]
Example to south
Near 30°: stop 30° past [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]]
At 30°, 15° bank: from east start at 203, from west at 157 [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]
Words used
The card "leads" turning north and "lags" turning south [[23:108|IFH 5-13]]
The compass lags when a turn starts from north and leads from south [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]; PHAK 8-27 uses the same words [[1:229|PHAK 8-27]]

body.p: Side by side near 40° north with 15° of bank: to north, rule A stops 35° early and rule B starts the roll-out about 47.5° early (40 + 7.5); to south, rule A goes 35° past and rule B 32.5° past (40 - 7.5) [[23:108|IFH 5-13]] [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

callout.text: Check Figure 7-35 against its text. The north half matches: turning left from east to north at 30° latitude, the compass reads 037 [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. The south half draws a left turn from west to south with the compass at 210°, short of south for that turn, while the text keeps the turn going until the compass passes south and gives 157° from the west and 203° from the east [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. Teach the text numbers.

Application: teach one rule, name its page, and check it with a timed turn. Rule B fits instrument training because it is tied to a 15° to 18° bank, the standard-rate bank of a trainer at 100 to 120 knots [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Tell the learner the other rule exists so a test question or another instructor does not surprise her.

check.q: Near 40° north your student turns left from east to north with 15° of bank. Where does rule A have her stop the turn, and where does rule B have her begin the roll-out?
check.a: Rule A stops the turn 15 + 20 = 35° early, near 035 [[23:108|IFH 5-13]]. Rule B starts the roll-out at the latitude plus half the bank, 40 + 7.5 = 47.5° early, about 047 to 048 [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. Both stop before north; they differ by about 12.5°.

chunks.title: Calibrating the turn coordinator, right and left

body.p: **Calibration of the miniature aircraft of the turn coordinator, right and left, using full panel and the clock.** Before timed turns, calibrate the turn coordinator to find out how accurate its indications are [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. The IFH procedure:

bullets: 1. Full panel, establish a standard-rate turn as shown by the turn coordinator [[23:182|IFH 7-21]], and note the bank on the attitude indicator at that indication [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].
2. As the sweep-second hand passes a cardinal point (12, 3, 6, 9), read the heading on the heading indicator [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].
3. Hold the indicated rate constant and note the heading change at 10-second intervals [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].
4. Compare with 30° per 10 seconds, the standard rate, and adjust the deflection [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].
5. Calibrate during turns in each direction, note any corrected deflections, and use them in all timed turns [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

body.p: Which way to adjust: more bank at the same speed gives a higher rate of turn [[23:88|IFH 4-11]]. So more than 30° in 10 seconds is a fast turn and needs a smaller deflection, and less than 30° needs a larger one. IFH 7-53, for glass, puts it in the matching order: if a 90° change takes more or less than 30 seconds, a deflection above or below the standard-rate line is needed to compensate [[23:214|IFH 7-53]]. Careful: IFH 7-21 words this sentence with "respectively larger or smaller", which read literally pairs "more" with "larger" [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]; teach the direction above.

Why the turn must be steady first: while the airplane rolls, the marks show a roll rate of 3° per second, not a turn rate; the turn coordinator shows the rate of turn only once the roll stops [[23:168|IFH 7-7]]. A rapid roll makes the miniature aircraft bank more steeply than a slow one [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]]. And once the roll stops the miniature aircraft shows only direction and rate of turn, so center the ball before trusting it [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

On glass with the PFD working: hold the indicated standard rate, start the timer as the compass card passes a cardinal heading and stop it at the next one. 90° should take 30 seconds; calibrate both directions and apply the result to all timed turns [[23:214|IFH 7-53]].

callout.text: Application: have the learner call the heading aloud at each 10-second mark while you watch the clock, then say the corrected picture in her own words ("right wing just below the mark"). A number she checked herself is one she will trust with the gyros covered.

check.q: Calibrating left, your student gets 36° in each 10-second interval at the standard-rate mark. What does she do?
check.a: 36° in 10 seconds is faster than standard rate, so she uses a smaller deflection, since less bank gives a lower rate at the same speed [[23:88|IFH 4-11]] [[23:214|IFH 7-53]]. Then she rechecks it and calibrates to the right as well [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

body.p: **Turn needle.** If the test airplane has a turn needle, it replaces the miniature aircraft of the turn coordinator for this Task (CFII PTS, Task F, footnote 1). The calibration and timed-turn procedures stay the same; the instrument changes.

body.p: Another IFH errata item belongs here. IFH 7-7 says "the turn-and-slip indicator provides both roll and turn indications"; FAA's errata (July 2, 2014) changes "turn-and-slip" to "turn coordinator" in that sentence [[23:168|IFH 7-7]]. Only the turn coordinator shows roll. The older turn-and-slip senses only rotation about the vertical axis and tells nothing of the roll, which in normal flight comes before the turn [[23:116|IFH 5-21]].

callout.text: Application: in an airplane with a needle, brief that it moves only once the airplane actually turns. A learner raised on the turn coordinator expects it to move with the roll-in and may chase it.

check.q: Your school's older trainer has a turn-and-slip marked 4 MIN TURN. Where is standard rate, and how do you calibrate it?
check.a: Two needle widths of deflection; on a 2 MIN instrument it is one width [[23:116|IFH 5-21]]. Calibrate it with the clock and the heading indicator just as for a turn coordinator [[23:182|IFH 7-21]], since the PTS puts the needle in place of the miniature aircraft (CFII PTS, Task F, footnote 1).

chunks.title: Timed turns: the numbers and the method

body.p: **Timed turns.** A timed turn uses the clock and the turn coordinator to change heading by a set number of degrees in a set time. At standard rate, 3° per second, the airplane turns 45° in 15 seconds; at half standard rate it turns 45° in 30 seconds [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. Divide the heading change by 3 for the seconds at standard rate [[23:214|IFH 7-53]], and by 1.5 at half standard rate.

body.p: The cross-check is the one for any turn to a heading, with the clock in place of the heading indicator: turn coordinator primary for bank, altimeter for pitch, airspeed indicator for power [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. Start the roll-in as the second hand passes a cardinal point, hold the calibrated standard-rate indication (half standard rate for small heading changes), and start the roll-out when the computed seconds are up. If roll-in and roll-out rates are the same, the entry and recovery time need not be counted [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. The glass section says the same: time from the start of the roll-in, roll out at the same rate, then make small corrections [[23:214|IFH 7-53]].

Pick the direction before the arithmetic. Turn the shortest way unless there is a reason not to. For a quick reciprocal, subtract 200 and add 20 from headings over 180, or add 200 and subtract 20 below 180: from 305 the reciprocal is 125, so a turn to 110 goes right [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

Check the result: full panel on the heading indicator; without it, on the compass after the turn, allowing for deviation [[23:182|IFH 7-21]], and only once straight, level and unaccelerated [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

callout.text: Seconds = degrees ÷ 3 at standard rate, degrees ÷ 1.5 at half standard rate. Roll in as the second hand hits 12, 3, 6 or 9; roll out at the same rate [[23:182|IFH 7-21]] [[23:214|IFH 7-53]].

check.q: Partial panel, your student must turn left from 030 to 360. Which rate and how long?
check.a: It is a 30° change, so half standard rate suits it [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]: 45° takes 30 seconds at half rate, so 30° takes 20 seconds [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

chunks.title: Compass turns, full panel and partial panel

body.p: **Procedures using full panel and partial panel performing compass turns to a specified heading.** Proficiency in compass turns depends on knowing the compass, smooth control technique and accurate bank and pitch control. Abrupt attitude or airspeed changes make the card move erratically and very hard to read [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. Partial panel here means the attitude gyro and heading indicator covered or inoperative [[23:162|IFH 7-1]].

Shortest direction [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]; work out the roll-out reading with one rule from the previous chunk

body.p: Application: for the first compass turns, leave the heading indicator uncovered but out of the learner's scan, and compare when she says she is on heading. Then cover it. A timed turn is the best cross-check: the IFH calls timed turns simpler because they need no allowance for compass errors [[23:214|IFH 7-53]], so when the compass and the clock disagree, first check that the compass was read straight, level and unaccelerated [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

callout.text: The bank is part of the rule. IFH 7-22 assumes 15° to 18° of bank [[23:183|IFH 7-22]], and the float tilts only to about 18° [[23:106|IFH 5-11]]. A learner who steepens the bank to hurry a compass turn makes the rule wrong and the card erratic.

check.q: Partial panel on south, your student turns right to west on the compass. When does the IFH say to start the roll-out?
check.a: About 5° before the compass reads west: turning to east or west from a southerly heading, the lead is about 5°; from a northerly heading it is 10° to 12° [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

chunks.title: Partial panel on glass: the standby compass and the timer

body.p: When the AHRS fails, all heading and attitude indications on the PFD are lost [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. The magnetic compass needs no other source of power and becomes the heading reference after an AHRS or magnetometer failure [[23:214|IFH 7-53]].

bullets: Timed turns over compass turns: after an AHRS or magnetometer failure the IFH uses timed turns because they are simpler; compass turns need the compass errors taken into account, timed turns do not [[23:214|IFH 7-53]].
Calibrate while the PFD works: 90° between two cardinal headings in 30 seconds, in both directions [[23:214|IFH 7-53]].

In the IFH example the AHRS failure also removes the slip/skid indicator and there is no standby turn coordinator; the compass is left, and it is not as useful as a turn coordinator or slip/skid indicator [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]. The standbys are an analog airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and magnetic compass [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].
As a backup to a failed HSI, the compass's erratic, unstable movement makes it more likely a supporting instrument [[23:199|IFH 7-38]].
Glass pilots tend to leave the standby instruments and the compass out of the scan [[23:161|IFH 6-28]].

body.p: The IFH does not say what bank reference to use for a timed turn when the AHRS failure also takes the turn rate indicator; in its example only the standby attitude indicator is left [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. FII.VI.B discusses this case; teach from the AFM supplement of the airplane you fly.

callout.text: Application: before every glass flight, have the learner point to the compass and the timer and say how she would calibrate. Ask again after the simulated failure, when the workload is real.

check.q: After a simulated AHRS failure your glass student asks why she should not just fly compass turns. What does the IFH say?
check.a: The IFH uses timed turns instead because they are simpler: compass turns require accounting for the compass errors, timed turns do not [[23:214|IFH 7-53]]. She still checks the result on the compass once straight and steady [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

chunks.title: Risk: failures, disorientation and safe practice

body.p: You teach these turns for a real failure. A vacuum failure can lead an unsuspecting pilot into a dangerous unusual attitude that needs a partial panel recovery, so pilots should practice flight without the attitude and heading indicators [[23:333|IFH 11-8]].

bullets: Recognize it: an inconsistency between the attitude indicator and the other instruments usually identifies a failure; compare the attitude indicator with the rate-of-turn indicator and VSI. In Figure 11-8 the airplane is level at 2,000 feet, not turning left as the failed gyros suggest [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].
Then: covering the failed instruments may help control and navigation; usually the next step is to advise ATC and, if necessary, declare an emergency [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

Long turns: in a prolonged constant-rate turn the inner ear stops sensing it, and the roll-out feels like a turn the other way; a pilot who rolls back in can lose control [[23:72|IFH 3-5]]. A 180° timed turn lasts a full minute at standard rate [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

Bank: any turn greater than standard rate counts as steep in instrument training [[23:183|IFH 7-22]], and the compass is erratic past about 18° [[23:106|IFH 5-11]]. Keep these turns at standard rate or less.

Lookout: simulated instrument flight needs a qualified safety pilot in the other control seat [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]]. Brief the positive exchange of flight controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]; FII.VI.A covers simulating failures safely.

callout.text: Application: cover instruments only in VMC, at a safe altitude, with a briefed plan, and say aloud that the failure is simulated. Uncover them at once if anything real happens. The PTS bars the examiner from simulating anything that may jeopardize safe flight (CFII PTS, Introduction); hold yourself to the same rule.

check.q: After a long partial panel timed turn your student rolls out and starts banking back the way she came. What is happening, and what do you say?
check.a: After a prolonged constant-rate turn the roll-out can feel like a turn the other way, and the pilot may reenter the turn [[23:72|IFH 3-5]]. Have her trust the turn coordinator and ball: miniature aircraft level means straight flight [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].

body.p: For S2 the examiner flies these errors on purpose. Say what you see, name the error, give the cause and the fix, and say how you would teach it. **Incorrect calibration procedures** and **improper timing** come first, because every later number depends on them.

head: Error
What you see
Cause
Fix and how you teach it
rows: Calibrating during the roll-in
Count started with the miniature aircraft on the mark but the heading barely moving
While rolling, the mark shows a roll rate, not a turn rate [[23:168|IFH 7-7]]
Start the 10-second checks once the bank is steady; show a brisk roll-in with the heading still
Calibrating one direction only
Timed turns accurate one way, off the other
The IFH calibrates in each direction [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]
Calibrate left and right and write both pictures down
Rate not held during the check
Heading change differs from interval to interval
The indicated rate must be held constant [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]
Trim first so the bank holds, then fly it again
Ball off center while calibrating
Ball off center during the check
Without a centered ball the turn may not come from bank [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Center the ball with rudder pressure [[23:186|IFH 7-25]], then recalibrate
Adjusting the wrong way
Turns get worse after the correction
More bank gives more rate at the same speed [[23:88|IFH 4-11]]
Fast turn: less deflection; slow turn: more [[23:214|IFH 7-53]]
Wrong start
Turn ends a few seconds early or late
Roll-in not begun as the second hand passes a cardinal point [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]
Wait for 12, 3, 6 or 9, then roll in
Unequal roll-in and roll-out
The same heading error after every turn
Entry and recovery time cancel only at equal rates [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]
Count aloud during roll-in and roll-out and match them
Wrong arithmetic
Turn twice or half as long as needed
Standard-rate seconds used at half standard rate, or the long way around [[23:182|IFH 7-21]] [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Say degrees, rate and seconds aloud before rolling in
Lost count
The student forgets when the turn began
Interruptions are a significant source of errors [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]
Note the start time; add a distraction such as reading the outside air temperature only once the turns work [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]

body.p: The IFH's errors during compass turns belong here too: faulty understanding or computation of lead and lag, and fixation on the compass during the roll-out. Until the airplane is straight, level and unaccelerated there is no need to read the heading, so cross-check for straight-and-level first and then check the turn [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

callout.text: Analyze before you correct. When the learner thinks aloud you can tell whether an error comes from a misconception or from motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. A wrong lead computation is a mistake, an error of thought; a forgotten start time is a slip, an error of action [[25:84|AIH 3-33]].

check.q: The examiner, as your student, starts the clock, rolls in slowly over several seconds and rolls out briskly. What do you name, and what is the fix?
check.a: Improper timing: entry and recovery time cancel only when roll-in and roll-out rates are the same [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. Match the two rates and practice full panel, checking each turn on the heading indicator [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

body.p: **Uncoordinated use of controls.** The ball shows whether the turn is coordinated [[23:88|IFH 4-11]], and it decides whether the turn coordinator can be read as bank: once the roll stops the miniature aircraft shows only direction and rate of turn, so unless the ball is centered do not assume the turn comes from a bank [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]. Miniature airplane tilted left with the ball to the right is a skid; tilted right with the ball to the right is a slip [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]. Aileron causes adverse yaw, so rudder is needed when entering and leaving turns for precise instrument flying [[23:88|IFH 4-11]]. Slips and skids also give false sensations of banking or tilting [[23:72|IFH 3-5]].

**Improper trim control.** The IFH trim faults in turns are not recognizing the need for a trim change because the cross-check is slow, not understanding how trim relates to attitude and power changes, chasing the VSI, and not trimming after power changes [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]. Not trimming during entry and after a prolonged turn is listed as a pitch fault [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. In a timed turn the clock competes for attention, and good trim leaves more time for other duties [[23:143|IFH 6-10]].

head: Error
What you see
Fix
rows: Aileron without rudder on roll-in or roll-out
Ball off center while the miniature aircraft moves
Coordinated aileron and rudder in the direction of turn [[23:180|IFH 7-19]]; center the ball with rudder [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]
Pressures held, not trimmed
Ball drifts in a long turn; altitude wanders
Check the ball throughout, especially with pressures held, and trim them off [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]
No retrim after a power change
Pitch creeps once the speed settles
Trim after every power change [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Chasing the VSI
Pitch follows each needle swing; a tight grip
Overcontrolling creates tension that hides the pressures to trim; relax, then trim [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]

body.p: Trimming in straight flight with the gyros covered, before and after the turn: aileron to level the miniature aircraft, rudder to center the ball, hold them, then release slowly while applying rudder trim, then aileron trim if fitted [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]. Rudder trim goes toward the side the ball is displaced [[23:143|IFH 6-10]].

callout.text: Application: when the examiner holds rudder in a timed turn, name it from the instrument, not the feel: "Ball right, miniature airplane left: a skid. I cannot use the turn coordinator for bank until the ball is centered."

check.q: In a partial panel timed turn to the left, the examiner holds left rudder; the ball moves right while the miniature aircraft sits on the mark. What do you name and fix?
check.a: Uncoordinated use of controls: miniature airplane left with the ball right is a skid [[23:169|IFH 7-8]], and with the ball off center the turn coordinator cannot be taken as bank [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]. Center the ball with rudder pressure and retrim [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

body.p: Plan from known to unknown and simple to complex [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Before learners combine tasks, they should be able to do each one reasonably well in isolation; fixation is often a sign that a task has not had enough practice on its own [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. Timing, calibration and compass reading are three separate skills before they are one maneuver.

head: Stage
What you do
rows: Ground

Compass construction and errors, the variation and deviation sums, both roll-out rules, the timed-turn arithmetic [[23:108|IFH 5-13]] [[23:183|IFH 7-22]] [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]; brief the exchange of controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
Preflight
Compass fluid and correction card, clock set and running, compass against the runway heading [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]
VMC, full panel
Show ANDS and the north and south turning errors; calibrate the turn coordinator left and right [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]
Timed turns, full panel
Check each one on the heading indicator [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]
Compass turns
Cardinal headings first, then others with interpolation [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]
Partial panel
Attitude gyro and heading indicator covered [[23:162|IFH 7-1]]; timed turns, then compass turns, each checked on the compass afterward [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]
Glass

Add load
A distraction such as resetting the clock, once the turns work [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]

body.p: Correcting errors: safety permitting, let the learner go part way into a mistake and find the way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Ask why the error happened; some errors need more practice, others point to a method that should change [[25:85|AIH 3-34]]. Teach checking, too: many aviation tasks offer a way to check the work [[25:84|AIH 3-33]], and here the compass checks the clock.

callout.text: Application: a wrong compass computation is a mistake, so reteach the rule on the kneeboard. Losing track of the start time is a slip, so practice and say the numbers aloud.

check.q: Your learner flies good timed turns but cannot explain why she rolled out early on a turn to north. How do you check her understanding?
check.a: Have her vary the maneuver, combine it with another or apply it elsewhere, for example a turn to south or from a different heading; a learner who lacks the principles usually cannot [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

body.p: In telling-and-doing, demonstrate in the same order you explained, and if the demonstration strays from the explanation, say so at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Then let the learner tell you what to do while you fly; it shows her understanding before she is busy flying [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
A talk-through in primary-and-supporting words, 110 knots true near 40° north:

bullets: "Calibration, full panel: turn coordinator on the left mark, ball centered. Second hand passing 12, heading 270. Ten seconds: 240, that is 30, so the mark is good. Now the same to the right [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]."
"Gyros covered. Turn coordinator primary for bank, altimeter for pitch, airspeed for power [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]."

"Right from 360 to 090 is 90°: 30 seconds at standard rate [[23:214|IFH 7-53]]. Second hand at 12: coordinated aileron and rudder, wing to the calibrated mark, ball centered [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]."
"A little back pressure as vertical lift drops, then trim [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Thirty seconds: roll out at the same rate as the roll-in [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]."
"Wings level, ball centered, altitude steady; now I read the compass. The card says 095 for 090 with the radios on [[23:187|IFH 7-26]] [[23:108|IFH 5-13]]."

"Compass turn left from east to north. Standard-rate bank is about 16°, so by IFH 7-22 I start the roll-out at about 048: 40 for latitude plus half the bank. The card lags toward north, so I stop early [[23:181|IFH 7-20]] [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]."
"Five degrees off after the roll-out: a small fix at half standard rate, about 3 seconds [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]."

body.p: In control-and-performance words the same turn is: set the bank and power, trim, cross-check the performance instruments, adjust [[23:135|IFH 6-2]] [[23:136|IFH 6-3]]. Application: with the attitude indicator covered, say "set the turn coordinator on the calibrated mark" where you would have said "set the bank".

callout.text: Application: the PTS lists an explanation that needs prompting as a typical reason for an unsatisfactory (CFII PTS, Unsatisfactory Performance). Rehearse this script aloud with a safety pilot until the arithmetic comes without thinking.

check.q: During your demo the 30 seconds run out, but the miniature aircraft sat a little past the mark the whole turn. What do you say and do?
check.a: Say so at once, because a demonstration that departs from the explanation should be acknowledged and explained [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Then read the compass once level and correct with a small half-standard-rate turn [[23:187|IFH 7-26]] [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

scenario.title: Partial panel on a hazy morning
scenario.setup: You are a CFII. Your instrument student, a private pilot, flies the school's fixed-pitch trainer at about 105 knots true: a six-pack panel with one engine-driven vacuum pump for the attitude and heading indicators, an electric turn coordinator, a magnetic compass with its correction card, and a panel clock with a sweep-second hand. The practice area is near 41° north. It is VMC with 6 miles in haze, and you are the safety pilot. Today: calibration, timed turns, then compass turns with the gyros covered.

questions.q: On the preflight, what do you have her check for this lesson?
questions.a: The compass full of fluid with the correction card in place and current, and the clock set and running; after start, the compass card moving freely and agreeing with a known heading such as the runway [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

questions.q: Calibrating full panel, she gets 34° in each 10-second interval to the right and 30° to the left at the standard-rate mark. What does she do with this?
questions.a: The left mark is good. To the right the turn is fast, so she uses a slightly smaller deflection, since less bank gives less rate at the same speed [[23:88|IFH 4-11]], rechecks it, and uses the corrected deflections in all timed turns [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

questions.q: Gyros covered, she must turn right from 360 to 135 at standard rate. Talk her through the timing.
questions.a: 135 ÷ 3 = 45 seconds [[23:214|IFH 7-53]]. Roll in as the second hand passes a cardinal point, hold the calibrated right deflection with the ball centered, roll out at the same rate when 45 seconds are up [[23:182|IFH 7-21]], then read the compass once straight, level and unaccelerated [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

questions.q: Next, a compass turn left from east to north. Her standard-rate bank is about 16°. Where does she start the roll-out, and why do you name the rule?
questions.a: By IFH 7-22: 41° of latitude plus half of 16°, so start rolling out at about 049 [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. By IFH 5-13 she would stop 15° plus half the latitude early: 15 + 20.5 = 35.5°, near 035 to 036 [[23:108|IFH 5-13]]. Naming the page lets her check it against a timed turn and not be thrown by the other rule.

questions.q: She rolls out, sees 010 on a swinging card and starts another turn at once. What error is it, and what do you teach?
questions.a: Fixation on the compass during the roll-out: cross-check for straight-and-level, unaccelerated flight before reading it [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]. Then correct with a small turn, using half standard rate for a small heading change [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

questions.q: In the debrief she says compass turns are confusing and asks why she needs both kinds of turn. What do you tell her?
questions.a: In most small airplanes the compass is the only direction instrument independent of other instruments and power, and knowing its errors lets her use it fully [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. Timed turns are simpler because they avoid the compass errors [[23:214|IFH 7-53]], and the compass then checks the result [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

skills.do: From the right seat, calibrate the turn coordinator (or turn needle) left and right with the full panel and the clock, then fly timed turns at standard and half standard rate and compass turns to an assigned heading, full panel and with the attitude and heading indicators covered, explaining in your chosen method's words the arithmetic, the primary instruments, the roll-out point and why the compass is read only once straight and steady.
skills.practice: Rehearse the talk-through in the last chunk under the hood with a qualified safety pilot [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]], in the order you brief it [[25:177|AIH 9-7]], and check each timed turn on the heading indicator before you trust it partial panel [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

skills.do: When the examiner calibrates during the roll-in, calibrates one way only, times from the wrong point, rolls out at a different rate, holds a skid or flies untrimmed, say what you see on the instruments, name the error, give the cause and the fix, and show how you would teach it.
skills.practice: Take turns with another applicant flying the errors in the two common-error chunks and the IFH compass-turn errors [[23:187|IFH 7-26]], naming each within a few seconds, never simulating anything that could jeopardize safe flight (CFII PTS, Introduction).

quiz.q: Partial panel on 270, your student levels off and lets the airspeed build. The compass swings toward north. What do you tell her?
options: The heading is drifting, so roll left to correct it now
On a west heading, acceleration shows a false turn north
The compass needs swinging; note it for maintenance
The turn coordinator has failed, so use the compass
quiz.why: On an east or west heading, acceleration gives a north turn indication and deceleration a south one [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]; the IFH memory aid is ANDS [[23:109|IFH 5-14]]. Swinging the compass reduces deviation, a different error [[23:107|IFH 5-12]]. Read the compass again once the speed is steady [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

quiz.q: On a north heading, your student starts a right turn toward east. What will the magnetic compass show at first?
options: A lag, or a turn to the left
A lead, more turn than is real
A correct turn to the right
A swing south from deceleration
quiz.why: On a north heading, when a turn is started east or west, the compass lags or shows a turn the other way; it leads when the turn starts from south and reads correctly when it starts from east or west [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

quiz.q: A study guide uses IFH Figure 5-20 to teach northerly turning error. What should you tell the CFII who wrote it?
options: It is the IFH's only correct drawing of turning error
The errata moved it to Chapter 7 as Figure 7-35
FAA's IFH errata says to disregard it as inaccurate
It applies only south of the magnetic equator
quiz.why: FAA's IFH errata (July 2, 2014) removes the IFH 5-13 references to Figures 5-20A and 5-20B and says to disregard Figure 5-20 because of inaccurate graphics [[23:108|IFH 5-13]] [[23:109|IFH 5-14]]. Figure 7-35 is a separate figure on IFH 7-22 [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

quiz.q: Calibrating right, your student holds the standard-rate mark and the heading changes only 24° in each 10-second interval. What does she do?
options: Fly a smaller deflection than the mark, then recheck
Accept it, since anything near 30° is close enough
Recalibrate only to the left, where the error began
Fly a larger deflection than the mark, then recheck
quiz.why: A true standard-rate turn changes 30° in 10 seconds [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. 24° is slow, and more bank gives more rate at the same speed [[23:88|IFH 4-11]], so she needs more deflection, which matches IFH 7-53's order: a 90° turn that takes more than 30 seconds needs a deflection above the standard-rate line [[23:214|IFH 7-53]]. A smaller deflection would slow it further. IFH 7-21's "respectively larger or smaller", read literally, pairs a slow turn with a smaller deflection [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]; that wording is backward.

quiz.q: Partial panel, your student turns from 090 to 180 at standard rate, rolling in and out at the same rate. How long does she time the turn?
options: 30 seconds
60 seconds
15 seconds
120 seconds
quiz.why: 90° at 3° per second is 30 seconds [[23:214|IFH 7-53]]. With equal roll-in and roll-out rates, the entry and recovery time need not be counted [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. 60 seconds would be the half-standard-rate time.

quiz.q: For a 30° heading correction your student chooses half standard rate. How long does she hold it?
options: 10 seconds, at 3° per second
15 seconds, at 2° per second
20 seconds, at 1.5° per second
30 seconds, at 1° per second
quiz.why: At half standard rate the airplane turns 45° in 30 seconds, 1.5° per second, so 30° takes 20 seconds; the IFH uses half standard rate for small heading changes [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. 10 seconds would be the standard-rate time.

quiz.q: Your trainer has a turn-and-slip indicator marked 2 MIN TURN. Where is the needle in a standard-rate turn?
options: Two needle widths off center
Halfway to the doghouse mark
Wherever the ball is centered
One needle width off center
quiz.why: On a 2 MIN instrument the needle one width either side of the center mark, aligned with a doghouse, is 3° per second; a 4 MIN instrument needs two widths [[23:116|IFH 5-21]]. The PTS footnote puts the needle in place of the turn coordinator for this Task (CFII PTS, Task F).

quiz.q: At 30° north with 15° of bank, your student turns left from east to north on the compass. By IFH 7-22, when does she start the roll-out?
options: At 360, right on north
At 037, before reaching north
At 323, after passing north
At 015, a little short of north
quiz.why: Turning to north, the lead is the latitude plus the normal roll-out lead: 30° plus half the 15° bank, so start at 037 [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. 323 is the IFH's point for the same turn from the west, and 360 ignores the turning error.

quiz.q: Partial panel on 180, your student turns right to 270 on the compass. By IFH 7-22, when does she start the roll-out?
options: About 5° before the card reads west
About 10° to 12° before it reads west
After the card passes west by the latitude
Exactly as the card reaches west
quiz.why: Turning to east or west from a southerly heading, start the roll-out about 5° early; from a northerly heading, about 10° to 12° early [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

quiz.q: Partial panel, your student stares at the compass during the roll-out and keeps chasing the swinging card. What do you coach?
options: Hold the bank until the card stops, then roll out
Steepen the bank so the turn ends before it swings
Read the card every second so that no swing gets missed
Fly straight and level first, then read the compass
quiz.why: Fixation on the compass during the roll-out is a listed error; until the airplane is straight, level and unaccelerated there is no need to read it, so cross-check straight-and-level first [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]. A steeper bank makes the card erratic past about 18° [[23:106|IFH 5-11]].

quiz.q: After a simulated AHRS failure, your glass student asks why the IFH flies timed turns rather than compass turns. What do you answer?
options: The compass fails along with the AHRS
Compass turns are not allowed under IFR
They are simpler, with no compass errors
The PFD timer needs the AHRS to keep running
quiz.why: The compass needs no other power and still gives heading; the IFH uses timed turns because they are simpler, with no compass errors to account for [[23:214|IFH 7-53]].

quiz.q: In a partial panel timed turn to the left, the miniature aircraft sits on the calibrated mark but the ball is well to the right. What do you name?
options: A slip; add left rudder until the ball is centered
A skid: do not read the turn coordinator as bank
Normal; the ball always moves outward in a turn
Precession of the turn coordinator's gyro
quiz.why: Miniature airplane tilted left with the ball displaced right is a skid [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]. Once the roll stops the turn coordinator shows only rate and direction, so unless the ball is centered do not assume the turn comes from a bank [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]. Center it with rudder on the side of the ball: right ball, right rudder [[23:169|IFH 7-8]].

final_quiz.q: Your student asks why the compass shows 33 to the right of N when she flies north, though east is on her right. What do you explain?
options: The compass is mounted backward to save space
Deviation moves the numbers 30° on north
Variation reverses the card east of Chicago
She sees the back of a card that stays still
final_quiz.why: The pilot sees the card from its backside: the card stays stationary while the housing and pilot turn around it [[23:106|IFH 5-11]]. That makes it easy to start a turn the wrong way [[23:110|IFH 5-15]].

final_quiz.q: Near 40° north your student turns to north on the compass. By the IFH 5-13 rule of thumb, how far before north does she stop the turn?
final_quiz.why: 15° plus half the latitude: 15 + 20 = 35° [[23:108|IFH 5-13]] [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]]. About 48° is the IFH 7-22 answer with a 16° bank [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]; 20° is half the latitude alone.

final_quiz.q: IFH 5-13's southerly turning example reads "15° + 15° + 30°". What is it meant to say, and where is it printed correctly?
options: Stop 15 + 15 = 30° after south, as PHAK 8-26 prints it
Stop 60° before reaching south, as IFH 7-22 has it
Stop 30° before reaching south, as the errata has it
Stop 15° past south, as the PHAK rule of thumb has it
final_quiz.why: The rule is 15° plus half the latitude, so near 30° latitude stop the turn 30° after passing the heading; the PHAK prints 15 + 15 = 30 [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]] [[23:108|IFH 5-13]]. The IFH errata does not list this typo; its compass items are the Figure 5-20 references.

final_quiz.q: Holding north partial panel, your student climbs, levels off and changes airspeed. What compass error does the IFH predict?
options: A false turn toward north as speed builds
None on a north or south heading
A false turn toward south in the climb
A lead of about the local latitude
final_quiz.why: When maintaining a north or south heading, no error results from diving, climbing or changing airspeed; acceleration error shows on east or west headings [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

final_quiz.q: Your student calibrated to the left only and now flies timed turns both ways. Which common error is it, and why does it matter?
options: Improper timing: the clock runs differently in each turn
Improper trim: rudder trim changes the rate the gyro shows
No error: one direction calibrates the whole instrument
Incorrect calibration: check each direction
final_quiz.why: Calibrate during turns in each direction, note the corrected deflections and apply them in all timed turns [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. Skipping one direction is an incorrect calibration procedure, PTS element K2a.

final_quiz.q: The examiner, playing your student, starts the 10-second calibration count while still rolling into the turn. What do you point out?
options: Calibration has to begin with the wings exactly level
The heading indicator lags in a roll, so wait a minute
While it is rolling, the mark shows roll rate, not turn rate
The clock has to be started at the 6 o'clock position
final_quiz.why: While the airplane is rolling, the turn coordinator's marks represent a roll rate of 3° per second; it shows the rate of turn once the turn has stabilized [[23:168|IFH 7-7]]. Start the 10-second checks in a steady turn [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]; a cardinal point can be 12, 3, 6 or 9.

final_quiz.q: In the IFH 7-53 example, how long does a standard-rate timed turn from 120° to 360° take?
options: 40 seconds
20 seconds
80 seconds
120 seconds
final_quiz.why: The heading change is 120°: 120 ÷ 3° per second = 40 seconds [[23:214|IFH 7-53]]. 80 seconds would be half standard rate [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

final_quiz.q: A turn-and-slip indicator in a faster airplane is marked 4 MIN TURN. What needle deflection is a standard-rate turn?
options: One needle width
Two needle widths
Half a needle width
Four needle widths
final_quiz.why: Some turn-and-slip indicators in faster aircraft are marked 4 MIN TURN; standard rate takes two needle widths, against one on a 2 MIN instrument [[23:116|IFH 5-21]].

final_quiz.q: Why does the IFH 7-22 compass roll-out rule call for 15° to 18° of bank?
options: It is the only bank a turn coordinator can show
Steeper banks reverse the northerly turning error
The FAA limits all instrument turns to 18° of bank
The lead or lag is about equal to the latitude in that band
final_quiz.why: With 15° to 18° of bank, the lead or lag to northerly and southerly headings is about the latitude [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. The float tilts only to about 18°, and steeper the readings are erratic [[23:106|IFH 5-11]].

final_quiz.q: In the IFH glass example, which standby instruments does the pilot have after an AHRS failure?
options: Turn coordinator, altimeter, compass and VSI
Only the magnetic compass and the clock
Airspeed, attitude, altimeter and compass
Attitude indicator and turn coordinator
final_quiz.why: The standbys are an analog airspeed indicator, attitude indicator, altimeter and magnetic compass, with no standby turn coordinator [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]; the failure also removes the slip/skid indicator in that example [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

final_quiz.q: Your student's vacuum pump fails for real in IMC. She keeps control and identifies the failed instruments. What does the IFH suggest next?
options: Cover them, advise ATC, declare if needed
Leave them in view to watch for recovery
Climb above the clouds before anything else
Turn off the turn coordinator to save power
final_quiz.why: Covering the failed instruments may help her keep control and navigate; usually the next step is to advise ATC and, if necessary, declare an emergency [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. Practicing flight without the attitude and heading indicators prepares for this [[23:333|IFH 11-8]].

final_quiz.q: Your student rolls into timed turns slowly and out of them briskly, and ends a little off heading each time. Why?
options: The clock should start after the roll-in ends
Entry and exit cancel only at equal rates
The turn coordinator lags in a slow roll-in
The compass leads in a quick roll-out
final_quiz.why: If the rates of roll-in and roll-out are the same, the entry and recovery time need not be counted [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]; unequal rates leave an error. The IFH times from the start of the roll-in, so starting the clock later is not the fix [[23:214|IFH 7-53]].

final_quiz.q: Partial panel, your student holds back pressure through a long timed turn instead of trimming. What does the IFH say to keep checking?
options: The compass, which corrects for the held pressure
Only the clock, since trim cannot change the timing
The suction gauge, since the gyros carry the load
The ball, especially with pressures held
final_quiz.why: Check the ball throughout the turn, especially if control pressures are held rather than trimmed off [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. Not trimming during entry and after a prolonged turn is a listed fault [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

final_quiz.q: Your student chases the VSI in timed turns and grips the yoke hard. Which listed trim fault is it, and why does it matter?
options: Calibration error: the VSI shows the rate of turn
Timing error: the VSI needle lags behind the clock
Overcontrolling: tension hides the pressures to trim
Acceleration error: pitch changes swing the compass
final_quiz.why: Chasing the vertical speed needle is a listed trim fault: overcontrolling leads to tension and prevents sensing the pressures to be trimmed off [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

final_quiz.q: Using the correction card in the figure, your student wants magnetic 120° with the radios on. What compass heading does she fly?
final_quiz.why: The card says steer 123 for 120 with the radios on; 125 is the radios-off figure [[23:108|IFH 5-13]].

final_quiz.q: Your student flies good timed turns, and you suspect she imitates rather than understands. What does the AIH suggest?
options: Have her vary it or combine it with another maneuver
Repeat the same turn until it comes out right three times
Give her a written test on all the compass errors first
Have her fly it once more without any briefing
final_quiz.why: When a learner may perform correctly without understanding, have her vary the maneuver slightly, combine it with other operations, or apply its elements to other maneuvers; one who lacks the principles usually cannot [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

final_quiz.q: Moving to a trainer with a turn needle, your student expects it to show her roll-in as the turn coordinator did. What do you correct?
options: The needle shows roll; the ball gives the turn rate
The needle shows the bank angle once the roll stops
Nothing; both instruments show roll and turn rate
The needle senses yaw only: turn, not roll
final_quiz.why: The turn-and-slip senses rotation only about the vertical axis and tells nothing of the roll [[23:116|IFH 5-21]]; it gives turn rate and trim [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]. IFH 7-7 says the turn-and-slip shows roll and turn, but FAA's IFH errata (July 2, 2014) changes that to turn coordinator [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].

takeaways: In most small airplanes the compass is the only direction instrument that needs no power or other instrument; teach it as a flight instrument, not just a reference for setting the heading indicator.
Variation and deviation are sums; acceleration, turning and oscillation errors are why the compass is read only straight, level and unaccelerated.
FAA's IFH errata says to disregard Figure 5-20. The IFH gives two roll-out rules, 5-13 and 7-22: teach one, name its page, mention the other.
Calibrate the turn coordinator, or the turn needle, both ways: hold the mark, check 30° per 10 seconds on the heading indicator, fast turn less deflection, slow turn more.
Timed turns: seconds = degrees ÷ 3 at standard rate and ÷ 1.5 at half standard rate; start on a cardinal point and roll in and out at the same rate.
Compass turns at 15° to 18° of bank: stop early turning to north and go past turning to south by about the latitude; to east or west lead 10° to 12° from north, 5° from south.
Name the common errors: calibrating while rolling or one way only, timing slips, ball off center, pressures not trimmed, and fixation on the compass.
cfi_notes: FAA's IFH errata (July 2, 2014, revising entries of February 12, 2014) removes the Figure 5-20A and 5-20B references from IFH 5-13 and says to disregard Figure 5-20 for inaccurate graphics [[23:108|IFH 5-13]] [[23:109|IFH 5-14]]. The PHAK prints the same drawing as Figure 8-36 [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]]; the errata covers only the IFH, but leave the PHAK copy out as well. The errata does not list the "15° + 15° + 30°" typo on IFH 5-13; PHAK 8-26 prints it as 15 + 15 = 30.

Two IFH roll-out rules: IFH 5-13 and PHAK 8-26 stop the turn 15° plus half the latitude early to north and late to south [[23:108|IFH 5-13]] [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]]; IFH 7-22 uses about the latitude plus (north) or minus (south) the normal roll-out lead, at 15° to 18° of bank [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. Near 40° with 15° of bank they differ by 12.5° turning north and 2.5° turning south. FII.II.A and AI.XI.D note the same split.

The lead and lag words differ too: IFH 5-13 and PHAK 8-26 call the northerly error a "lead" of the card, while IFH 7-22 and PHAK 8-27 say the compass lags when a turn starts from north and leads from south [[23:108|IFH 5-13]] [[23:183|IFH 7-22]] [[1:229|PHAK 8-27]]. Teach the action, which all of them agree on: turning to north stop early, turning to south go past.

Figure 7-35 does not match its own text on the south half: it draws a left turn from west to south with the compass at 210°, while the text rolls out at 157° from the west and 203° from the east [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. The north half (037 from the east) matches. This is not in the errata.

IFH 7-21 says a turn of "more than or less than 30°" in 10 seconds needs "a respectively larger or smaller deflection" [[23:182|IFH 7-21]], which read literally is backward. IFH 4-11 (more bank, more rate) and IFH 7-53 (90° taking more or less than 30 seconds: deflect above or below the line to compensate) give the working direction: a fast turn needs less deflection, a slow turn more [[23:88|IFH 4-11]] [[23:214|IFH 7-53]].

Another errata item matters for the turn needle footnote: IFH 7-7 says the "turn-and-slip indicator provides both roll and turn indications"; the errata changes it to "turn coordinator" [[23:168|IFH 7-7]]. The needle senses yaw only [[23:116|IFH 5-21]].

The IFH has two calibration methods: round dials check 30° every 10 seconds on the heading indicator [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]; glass times 90° between two cardinal headings, which should take 30 seconds [[23:214|IFH 7-53]]. Both calibrate each direction. The PTS wants it done with full panel and the clock, so do it before covering anything.

Expect the examiner to ask for the compass errors, a calibration each way, the seconds for a heading change at standard and half standard rate, and a roll-out point at the local latitude, and to fly an early clock start, unequal roll rates, a skid or an untrimmed turn for S2. Under the Area NOTE, Task F may not be picked at all, but Task H always is (CFII PTS, Area VI NOTE).

Application: the IFH compass-turn numbers are for 15° to 18° of bank [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. Keep half standard rate for small timed corrections [[23:182|IFH 7-21]] rather than for compass turns, since no source gives lead or lag values for shallower banks.
gaps: No source says whether the IFH 5-13 "15° plus half the latitude" point is where the roll-out begins or where the wings should be level; IFH 7-22 says its figure includes the normal roll-out lead [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].
No source gives compass lead or lag values for banks outside 15° to 18°, such as half standard rate; for headings other than the cardinal ones the IFH only says to interpolate [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].
No source gives a tolerance for an acceptable calibration (for example 29° against 30° in 10 seconds), and the PTS gives no heading tolerance for this Task.

The deviation values, where the compass and clock are mounted, and whether the airplane has a turn coordinator or a turn needle (2 MIN or 4 MIN) come from the airplane and its correction card, not the handbooks.

No source says what bank reference to use for a timed turn when an AHRS failure also removes the turn rate indicator; in the IFH example only the standby attitude indicator is left [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. Check the AFM supplement.

activities.title: Which compass error is it?
activities.intro: Tap a description, then the compass error or limit it describes.

pairs.l: The same on every heading along an isogonic line
Different on each heading; what is left goes on the correction card
On east or west, speeding up shows a turn toward north
The card swings back and forth around the heading
Starting a turn from north, the card first shows a turn the other way
Readings become erratic past about 18° of bank

activities.why: Variation and deviation [[23:107|IFH 5-12]] [[23:108|IFH 5-13]]; acceleration and oscillation [[23:109|IFH 5-14]]; turning error [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]; tilt limit [[23:106|IFH 5-11]].

activities.title: True or false: what the compass does in flight
activities.intro: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

cards.s: On a north heading, climbing or changing airspeed causes no compass error.
cards.why: True. When maintaining a north or south heading, no error results from diving, climbing or changing airspeed [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

cards.s: On an east heading, slowing down shows a turn toward north.
cards.why: False. Deceleration shows a turn toward south; acceleration shows north (ANDS) [[23:183|IFH 7-22]] [[23:109|IFH 5-14]].

cards.s: When a turn is started from an east or west heading, the compass shows it correctly.
Turning errors grow as the airplane gets closer to either magnetic pole.
cards.why: True. The error is amplified with proximity to either pole [[23:108|IFH 5-13]] [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]].

cards.s: Deviation changes with the airplane's geographic location.
cards.why: False. Deviation changes with heading, not with location; variation is the one tied to location [[23:107|IFH 5-12]].

cards.s: An electrically heated windshield can cause compass deviation of as much as 40°.

activities.title: Compass roll-out points, by rule
activities.intro: Each item names its rule: IFH 7-22 (latitude plus or minus half the bank) or IFH 5-13 (15° plus half the latitude). Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: IFH 7-22: 30° N, 15° bank, turning left from east to north. At what compass reading do you start the roll-out?
IFH 7-22: 30° N, 15° bank, turning right from east to south. At what compass reading do you start the roll-out?
IFH 7-22: 40° N, 16° bank, turning left from east to north. At what compass reading do you start the roll-out?
IFH 7-22: 40° N, 16° bank, turning left from west to south. At what compass reading do you start the roll-out?
items.why: Keep turning until the compass passes south by the latitude minus the normal lead: 180 - (40 - 8) = 148. The IFH's own example, 30° and 15° of bank from the west, gives 157 [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

items.q: IFH 5-13 rule: 40° N, turning to north. How many degrees before north do you stop the turn?
IFH 5-13 rule, as PHAK 8-26 prints it: 30° N, turning to south. How many degrees past south do you stop the turn?

activities.why: Rule B from IFH 7-22 [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]; rule A from IFH 5-13 and PHAK 8-26 [[23:108|IFH 5-13]] [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]].

activities.title: Calibrating the turn coordinator, the IFH way
activities.intro: Put the steps in order, first to last, then tap Check.
steps: Full panel, roll into a turn with the miniature aircraft on the standard-rate mark
Let the roll stop, center the ball and note the bank on the attitude indicator
As the second hand passes 12, 3, 6 or 9, read the heading indicator
Hold the indicated rate and note the heading change every 10 seconds
Compare with 30° per 10 seconds and adjust the deflection
Repeat in the other direction and note both corrected deflections
activities.why: Procedure from IFH 7-21 [[23:182|IFH 7-21]], with the bank noted per IFH 7-20 [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. While rolling, the marks show roll rate, so let the turn stabilize first [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].

activities.title: How many seconds? Timed turns at standard and half standard rate
activities.intro: Work out how long to hold each timed turn, with roll-in and roll-out at the same rate. Type your answer in seconds.

items.q: Half standard rate, a 30° heading change.
items.why: Half standard rate turns 45° in 30 seconds, 1.5° per second: 30 ÷ 1.5 = 20 [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

items.q: Standard rate, 120 to 360, the IFH glass example.
Standard rate, 305 to 110 the shortest way.
items.why: The reciprocal of 305 is 125, so turn right [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]: 55° to 360 plus 110 is 165°, and 165 ÷ 3 = 55.

items.q: Calibration showed 36° per 10 seconds at the mark you meant to use. How long would a 90° turn take at that deflection?
items.why: 3.6° per second: 90 ÷ 3.6 = 25 seconds, so the turn would overshoot if timed for 30. That is why the IFH corrects the deflection before timed turns [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

activities.why: 45° in 15 seconds at standard rate and in 30 seconds at half standard rate [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]; heading change ÷ 3 = seconds at standard rate [[23:214|IFH 7-53]].

activities.title: A vacuum failure: what each instrument does now
activities.intro: The attitude and heading indicators in this panel have failed. Drag each label to its numbered pin.

pins.label: Primary for bank in a timed turn: hold the calibrated mark, ball centered
Primary for pitch in a timed turn
Primary for power in a timed turn
Flagged: the clock takes its place in a timed turn
Flagged: shows a left bank, yet the airplane is level
Compare it with the attitude indicator to find the failure

activities.why: Primary instruments in a timed turn and the clock in place of the heading indicator from IFH 7-21 [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]; comparing the attitude indicator with the rate-of-turn indicator and VSI, and the airplane actually level at 2,000 feet, from IFH 11-7 [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

activities.title: Which common error is it?
activities.intro: Tap each thing the examiner does, then the PTS common error it shows.

items.t: Starts the 10-second checks while still rolling in
Rolls in before the second hand reaches a cardinal point
Uses 3° per second for a half-standard-rate turn
Rolls in slowly, rolls out briskly
Ball well outside the turn with the miniature aircraft on the mark
Aileron without rudder on the roll-in
Holds back pressure through a long turn instead of trimming
Never retrims after the power change at roll-in

activities.title: A partial panel lesson, one call at a time
activities.intro: Your instrument student flies a six-pack trainer with a vacuum-driven attitude and heading indicator and an electric turn coordinator, near 40° north. It is VMC and you are the safety pilot.

steps.s: Before you cover anything, she wants to go straight to compass turns.
options: Calibrate the turn coordinator left and right with the full panel first
Cover the gyros now; calibration can wait until the next lesson
Skip calibration, since the standard-rate mark is set at the factory
Calibrate one direction only, since both sides of the gyro are the same
steps.why: Calibrate before timed turns, in each direction, with the full panel [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

steps.s: Gyros covered. She must turn from 180 to 270 and asks how long.
options: About 45 seconds at standard rate
30 seconds, rolling in on a cardinal point
60 seconds at standard rate, to be safe
Until the compass reads exactly 270
steps.why: 90° ÷ 3 = 30 seconds, rolling in as the second hand passes a cardinal point [[23:182|IFH 7-21]] [[23:214|IFH 7-53]].

steps.s: In the turn the ball drifts to the outside, and she says the turn feels fine.
options: Trust the feel, since the turn coordinator is on the mark
Add rudder toward the turn to tighten it up
Name the skid and center the ball with rudder
Ignore the ball during timed turns
steps.why: Ball to the outside of the turn is a skid [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]; center it with rudder pressure [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. Slips and skids give false sensations, so the feel cannot be trusted [[23:72|IFH 3-5]].

steps.s: Next, a compass turn right from west to north with about 16° of bank. She plans to roll out when the card reads N.
options: Fine, the compass is accurate on north
Start the roll-out at about 312, by IFH 7-22
Start the roll-out at about 048, by IFH 7-22
Roll out after the card passes north by 40°
steps.why: Turning to north the roll-out lead is the latitude plus the normal lead: 40 + 8 = 48° before north, about 312 from the west [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]. 048 is the point when turning from the east. By IFH 5-13 she would stop 35° early [[23:108|IFH 5-13]].

steps.s: She rolls out and stares at the swinging compass while the altitude drifts.
options: Fly straight and level first, then read the compass
Keep watching the card until it has settled completely
Turn back toward north until the card stops moving
Climb a little so the card stops swinging
steps.why: Fixation on the compass during the roll-out is a listed error; cross-check straight-and-level first, then check the heading [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

steps.s: Debrief: she asks which turns to use if the vacuum pump really fails in IMC.
options: Compass turns only, since timed turns need the gyros
No turns at all until the airplane is back in VMC
Steep turns, to get each heading change over quickly
Timed turns on the turn coordinator, checked on the compass
steps.why: With the attitude and heading indicators gone, timed turns use the clock and turn coordinator, and the compass checks the result once level [[23:182|IFH 7-21]] [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]. Then advise ATC and declare an emergency if needed [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].
